Senses.PreferredTarget: to appear in the world
Senses.Note: Across the collected corpus the expression has 7,523 exact occurrences in 428 distinct works. In this sense the subject is a buddha, sage, or group of awakened teachers appearing in an age. It is distinct from the institutional use for a Chan teacher taking an abbacy. One authored witness and one independently deployed lamp recension establish the sense; the lamp does not control the translation.

Senses.Explanation: 出世 means to appear in the world when its subject is a buddha, sage, or group of awakened teachers emerging in an age. Yongming Yanshou asks whether even a thousand sages appearing would leave the reader free of doubt. Nanyang Huizhong says that the buddhas continually appear and continually speak the dharma to free people. The phrase marks their public emergence and activity; it does not in these clauses mean withdrawing from ordinary life.

Senses.Explanation: 出世 also means to take up an abbacy: to emerge into public teaching by accepting responsibility for a monastery. Yuanwu Keqin presents this as something a mature teacher is pushed into only when circumstances require it, so that the teacher responds to conditions and opens the way for others. Gulin Qingmao uses the term when naming Liao'an Qingyu's first appointment at Kaifu, followed by his move to Benjue. A lamp biography says that Zuyin Zhifu took up the seat at Changlu and immediately records his inaugural hall address. In this institutional use, 出世 names entry into public responsibility, not the appearance of a buddha in an age.

Senses.Explanation: The standing dare of the Chan hall: whoever claims the matter steps out of the ranks and tries to say it, while the master stakes the seat on the answer. Yunmen Wenyan asks whether anyone has awakened and dares them to come out and say it, answering in their place with the bond of raising a son, Wuzu Fayan raises Deshan's no-questions-tonight ruling and dares any man who disregards his life to come out and say it, promising to meet the old man on the assembly's behalf if none does, Tianyin Yuanxiu sets aside those without proof at Linji's rank-pulling and dares those with proof to come out and say it, verse-breaking the gold-for-six-dusts trade when none appears, and Hanyue Fazang, raising beans and melons on Dengwei, dares any true bare-boned mountain man to come out and say it, then rests on opening fields to store summer water. Fushi Tongxian dares anyone in the crowd who matches the seed-time season to come out and say it, answering himself with white egrets over the misty paddies and orioles in the summer trees, Baiyu Jingsi asks the turning-around phrase outside the night-bright curtain and dares whoever says it in accord to come out — one monk barely steps out and he leaves the seat, Yulin Tongxiu sets his new temple's answers against the old man's urgent-state replies and dares whoever knows the landing place, same or different, to come out and say it, and Zishui dares whoever knows their own wrong to come out and say it, else the Tianhuang will drum his two skins while the crowd lends all ears and he leaves the seat.

Senses.Explanation: ‘To stand out takes a gifted person; to match an opponent takes a lion's cub’ summons someone who can meet a demanding encounter. The pair often follows a direct challenge to the assembly, turning an admired ideal into a test of who will answer. Feiyin Tongrong asks for a line of solitary freedom at the end of a release-day sermon. Yongji Rong asks whether a bold warrior will come from the assembly to fight one round. Miyun Yuanwu cites the pair after warning that the decisive move does not suit ordinary expectations. Muyun Tongmen revisits an old exchange and strikes his staff as he gives the couplet. Yinyuan Longqi says he would withdraw three steps before a person capable of such acts, then names that person with the lion image. Yichu Wuyuan gives the saying after asking what a monk gains, but allows that someone may laugh at his answer and make him withdraw. Lianyue Daozheng shouts it at a shaving ceremony to press the newly ordained person's encounter with the first meaning.

Senses.Explanation: Getting free of the situation may be easy; speaking from complete freedom is harder. The line distinguishes a way out from full, unconfined expression. Current deployments include Juelang Daosheng in J34nB311, Baochi Xuanzong in J35nB337, Hengxiulin Falin in J36nB355, and Jiguang Huo in J36nB367. The full paired image remains the lexical unit. The sources do not treat departure from a place as the same as complete liberation.

Senses.Explanation: An emergence point or way out in Chan speech is the place from which a practitioner can move freely beyond a caught position. Yuanwu uses the word for a sentence that offers release; an unnamed monk asks Yunmen where buddhas emerge. Miyun challenges his assembly to find such a way, Guxue contrasts the living escape with a dead road, Lianyue speaks of the Pang family distinct ways, and Chaozong places the phrase in his own Huangbo verse. Retained public meaning is supported by independent present uses in recorded discourse.

Jiqi replaces the two Buddha names with ox-head and horse-face gate figures. Yushan sets the old wording against Longji’s question in a current sermon. A case collection preserves another reply that turns the outside and inside into ordinary landscape and buildings. The line brings the named Buddhas to a doorway, where the later questions refuse a fixed label.

Senses.Explanation: Alert or wide-awake. The headword is attested. One major use is the command “stay awake” or “stay alert” (惺惺著, 169 occurrences). Ruiyan Shiyan's case has him call “Master!” to himself, answer “Yes!”, then say, “Stay awake; after this do not be fooled by anyone” (主人公……諾……惺惺著，以後莫被人瞞). The same word describes an alert person: Tianyin Yuanxiu contrasts an alert person, for whom moving, not moving, or both are acceptable, with a person who is not alert, for whom none is acceptable (惺惺底人……未惺惺底人). A second major use is the fixed pair “still and alert” or “alert and still” (寂寂惺惺 / 惺惺寂寂, 47 / 36 occurrences). Yongjia Xuanjue's Verse on Stopping defines alert as not producing the signs of dull abiding or blank indeterminacy (惺惺謂不生昏住無記等相), then ranks alert-and-still as right, blank-and-still as wrong, still-and-alert as right, and scattered-and-alert as wrong (惺惺寂寂是，無記寂寂非，寂寂惺惺是，亂想惺惺非). Later records also criticize these uses. Zhanran Yuancheng reports that all quarters called Ruiyan's self-address “playing with spirit-ghosts” (諸方謂其弄精魂). Fangrong Tongxi reverses the case by saying Ruiyan's house-master called Ruiyan rather than the reverse. Haiyin Zhaoru names still-and-alert among fetters, paired with torpor and scattering (被寂寂惺惺、昏沉散亂縛). The entry therefore keeps the attested gloss “alert” while preserving both the formulas and the named criticisms.

Senses.Explanation: Stay keenly alert is a direct command to remain awake to deception. Chan records preserve it most famously as Ruiyan Shiyan's call-and-response with himself, then reuse the command in public addresses to assemblies, a named layman, and even the monastery's guardian spirits. Ruiyan Shiyan calls 'master of the house,' answers himself, commands 'stay keenly alert,' and adds 'later, do not be deceived by anyone.' The repeated answers make the command a public case of self-address rather than an abstract adjective. Dahui Zonggao reenacts the call with his own name and reports laughter, while Yikui Yuankui gives the warning directly to his assembly. Yikui also stages an objector turning the same command back upon him before criticizing his speech. Yongjue Yuanxian addresses the monastery guardians with the command, and elsewhere raises the whisk and names Layman Zixuan before saying it. These uses retain the imperative force while moving it beyond Ruiyan's original self-call. The phrase does not itself name a silent exercise or an altered state. Its observable Chan bend is its reusable interview command: a person is called to alertness and the warning against being deceived follows or remains understood.

Senses.Explanation: Glaring with open eyes inside a coffin is a reaction that occurs after the person is already enclosed as dead. Chan masters use the image for a shout, display, or attempted recovery that arrives too late to alter the encounter; several immediately add that it is useless or that the falcon has already crossed to Silla. Dongta Xi says that even overturning the seat would only be glaring in the coffin and asks what use that has. Tian’an Sheng answers an interlocutor’s shout with the phrase. Feiyin Tongrong gives it after a boast of stepping beyond heaven and earth, then says the questioner invites laughter. Shouchang Benlai applies it after a beaten monk sticks out his tongue. Shending Yikui answers a shout with the phrase in a cremation question.

Senses.Explanation: The Mount Wutai road-woman of the Chan records: the case figure — pointed straight ahead by, sent off with a mocking word, claimed seen-through by Zhaozhou, graded one-sided by the raisers, and crowned the hidden veteran of the forest. Jingting Dezong raises the case in his own voice — a monk asks the woman the way to the terrace mountain, she says straight ahead, the monk has barely walked when she sends him off: a fine monk, gone like that again — and closes the pair as two hole-less iron mallets, asking which of the two was really seen through, Yanju Deshen verses her holding her charm in the wind: seen through — when did she ever get her head out? The mountain still, the water slow, an iron snake lying across the old road, its poison air pressing the traveler with dread, Wuqu Rukong counts her pointing straight ahead as too many curves — seen through for her sake, it all turns blurry; for no reason she babbles on level ground, vexing the travelers out of their even road, and Wuhuan Xingchong rules her straight-ahead one smooth even road, and the seeing-through for the monk's sake a trifle too small — she has walked the rough and the smooth both, and sits at ease in her terrace-mountain home. Wuming Huijing sets her hiding the spring colors, showing the autumn light — eyes must not mirror her, even wisdom cannot measure her; home, she never climbs the Chang'an road, letting wind, flowers, snow, and moon drift as they will, Shiqi Tongyun raises the case to the verdict — the terrace-mountain woman, I have seen her through for you — and turns it: the old man of Zhaozhou, eyes blazing through the four quarters, saw one side only; saying he saw the woman through, he little knew he himself was seen through by her — and then asks what of the crowd before him, all of them the terrace-mountain woman: who will see them through?, Meixi Fudu verses her as the snow-spirit flaunting its strength, drifts banking on the old path and quiet stream — till a three-foot fire sweeps the mountain and it all turns to one lump of ice, and Fushi Tongxian himself tests the recluse Xuecen with the case: Zhaozhou's seeing-through of the terrace-mountain woman — where exactly is the seeing-through place? — and gets the answer: the night-cuckoo cries blood till midnight, and still the east wind cannot be called back.

Senses.Explanation: An egret is the white water bird repeatedly placed among snow, moonlight, white reeds, lotus, and mist in Chan verse and hall imagery. Danxia Zichun says an egret standing in snow is not the same color and pairs moonlight with reed flowers in a similar distinction. Changqing Huileng puts the bird into a reed-flower thicket where snow and moon together still do not reach it. Other poems retain the literal bird's flight, stance, fishing, and pale surroundings. The recurring white-on-white comparison makes sameness-with-difference observable without replacing the animal.

Senses.Explanation: A white egret standing in snow places one white form against another without making bird and setting identical. Danxia states the point directly: the egret in snow is not the same color, just as moonlight and reed flowers are not simply alike. Qingxian gives the line as an answer, and an interlocutor presents it to Dahui for testing. The capping verse varies the comparison by asking how the egret in snow differs from the bright moon. Across these uses, close likeness is visible without collapsing the things distinguished.

Senses.Explanation: ‘A white egret standing in snow is not the same hue; bright moonlight and reed flowers are not alike’ presents two nearly white scenes whose parts still differ. Masters use the verse to test whether a listener can see beyond easy visual sameness. Yuanwu uses the old line after an image of a snow lion and denies that the case is simply about one color. Xueyan makes it part of a new verse and warns that a family-resemblance reading already misses the way. Xuzhou gives the couplet after a staff gesture and a question about seeing Samantabhadra. Wenmu repeats Danxia's earlier use, then adds his own verse about the treasure not recognized by ordinary sight.
